A2.text:
Nigar is twenty. On Saturday night, she took her little brother, Ali, to a big concert on the Boulevard. Ali is eight. He wore his favourite yellow hat.

There were thousands of people. The crowd was very big, and it was overwhelming. There was no space to walk. They waited in a long queue for ice cream.

After the concert, everybody walked to the metro. Nigar held Ali's hand, but people started to bump into her. When she looked down, Ali was not there!

Nigar was very scared. She tried to push through the people. “Ali! Ali!” she shouted. But the music was loud.

Then she remembered the yellow hat. “He will stand out in a crowd,” she thought. She climbed on a bench and looked around. There! A small yellow hat was near the information tent.

She ran there. Ali was eating his ice cream with a police officer.

“I did not follow the crowd,” Ali said. “You told me: if you are lost, go to the tent.”

At that moment, there was an announcement: “Nigar, your brother Ali is at the information tent.”

Nigar laughed and hugged him. Then they took the metro home. The train was packed. They were packed like sardines, but Nigar did not care. She held Ali's hand all the way.

B1.text:
When Nigar promised to take her eight-year-old brother Ali to the free summer concert on the Boulevard, she had no idea that half of Baku would have the same plan. By eight o'clock, the crowd stretched from the Puppet Theatre to the Carpet Museum, and the noise and lights were almost overwhelming. Ali, in his bright yellow bucket hat, loved every minute.

They spent forty minutes in a queue for ice cream, then found a small space near a palm tree to watch the show. Before they left the house, Nigar had made Ali repeat one rule: “If we get separated, go to the information tent and wait.”

The trouble started when the concert ended and thousands of people moved towards the metro at the same time. Nigar was holding Ali's hand tightly until someone bumped into her from behind. She lost her balance for a second, and when she looked down, her hand was empty.

Panic hit her like cold water. She tried to push through the wall of people, calling his name, but nobody could hear her over the music still coming from the speakers.

Then she thought of the hat. If anything could stand out in a crowd, it was that ridiculous yellow hat. She climbed onto a bench and searched the sea of heads. There — a small yellow dot, moving steadily in the opposite direction from everyone else.

She jumped down and fought her way towards it. When she reached the information tent, Ali was sitting on a plastic chair, finishing his ice cream next to a police officer.

“Everyone was going to the metro,” he explained calmly. “But you said don't follow the crowd. You said go to the tent.”

Just then, an announcement came over the speakers: “Would Nigar please come to the information tent? Ali is waiting for her.”

On the way home, the train was packed like sardines. Nigar didn't mind. She didn't let go of Ali's hand once.

B2.text:
When Nigar agreed to take her eight-year-old brother Ali to the free summer concert on the Boulevard, she had pictured a pleasant evening by the sea. She had not pictured the other two hundred thousand residents of Baku who had evidently formed the same plan. By eight o'clock the crowd extended from the Puppet Theatre all the way to the Carpet Museum, and the combination of noise, heat and flashing stage lights was close to overwhelming. Ali, who had refused to leave home without his luminous yellow bucket hat, thought it was the greatest night of his life.

They queued for forty minutes for ice cream and then claimed a scrap of space beside a palm tree. Before setting out, Nigar had drilled him on one rule until he could recite it with his eyes closed: “If we get separated, go to the information tent and stay there.”

The real test came at the end, when the entire audience surged towards the metro at once. Nigar kept a firm grip on Ali's hand right up to the moment someone bumped into her from behind. She stumbled for a split second, and when she regained her footing, her hand was holding nothing at all.

Fear flooded through her. She tried to push through the solid wall of bodies, shouting his name, but her voice vanished beneath the music still pounding from the speakers.

Then a thought surfaced through the panic: the hat. If there was a single object in Baku designed to stand out in a crowd, it was that absurd, glowing yellow hat. She scrambled onto a bench and scanned the moving sea of heads — and there it was, a small bright dot travelling steadily against the current.

She clambered down and battled her way after it. At the information tent she found Ali perched on a plastic chair, finishing his ice cream under the supervision of a police officer, as composed as a businessman waiting for a meeting.

“Everyone else was going to the metro,” he informed her. “But you said never follow the crowd. You said go to the tent.”

At that moment an announcement crackled across the Boulevard: “Would Nigar please come to the information tent, where her brother Ali is waiting.”

The train home was packed like sardines, every passenger pressed against three others. Nigar didn't notice. She didn't loosen her grip on Ali's hand once.

podcast.title: A girl in a red hat

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: Do you like crowds? Guess: who got lost on New Year's Eve?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is crowds and public places. Leyla, how was your trip this morning?
Terrible. The metro was packed. We were packed like sardines.
[laugh] At eight in the morning it's always the same. Nobody has any space.
And everyone is pushing. I almost couldn't get out at my station.
In England people make a queue for everything. Even for the bus.
Really? Here, a queue is more like… a suggestion. [chuckle]
I learned that in my first week in Baku. I stood politely, and ten people walked in front of me.
Big crowds can be scary, too. Last New Year, we took my niece Aysu to the boulevard for the fireworks.
Oh, that's a huge crowd.
Thousands of people. I looked at the sky for one second, and Aysu was gone.
No! What did you do?
I ran to the information point. A minute later there was an announcement: "A little girl in a red hat is looking for her aunt."
Phew. Good thing she had a red hat. A red hat helps you stand out in a crowd.
Exactly. Now she always wears something bright.
For me, the worst is a shopping centre on Saturday. The music, the lights, the people — it's overwhelming.
So why do you go?
Because my friends go. I just follow the crowd. [laugh]
And your half marathon? There will be a crowd there too.
That's a good crowd. When people cheer, I run faster. And I always bump into friends at the finish.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: do you love crowds or avoid them — and where is the most crowded place in your city?
Mine is the shopping centre on Saturday. See you next time!
Bye for now!
